etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English crane, from Old English cran (“crane”), from Proto-West Germanic *kran, from Proto-Germanic *kranô (“crane”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”).

Cognate with Scots cran (“crane”), Dutch kraan (“crane”), German Kran (“crane”). The mechanical devices are named from their likeness to the bird.

definitions.definition: Any bird of the family Gruidae, large birds with long legs and a long neck which is extended during flight.

quote.citation: 1876, "Burmah" in the  Encyclopædia Britannica, 9th ed., Vol. IV, p. 552:
quote.text: Aquatic birds of various kinds are very numerous, such as geese, darters (Flotus melanogaster), scissor-bills (Rhynchops nigra), adjutants (Leptoptilos argala), pelicans, cormorants, cranes (Grus antigone, in Burmese gyoja), whimbrels, plovers, and ibises.

definitions.definition: (US, dialect) Ardea herodias, the great blue heron.
A mechanical lifting machine or device, often used for lifting heavy loads for industrial or construction purposes.

quote.citation: 2000, Bob Foster, Birdum or Bust!, Henley Beach, SA: Seaview Press, page 111:
quote.text: Large cranes were virtually non-existent in the areas I worked with this truck, so we jacked everything on and off[.]

definitions.definition: An iron arm with horizontal motion, attached to the side or back of a fireplace for supporting kettles etc. over the fire.
A siphon, or bent pipe, for drawing liquors out of a cask.
(nautical) A forked post or projecting bracket to support spars, etc.; generally used in pairs.
